title: First discovery session: three US small-business administrative problems

history.reason: Session opened under the first-session brief (issue #7)
Three problem records documented with sources, counterevidence, and unknowns; no validation claimed

objective: Identify three distinct US small-business administrative customer problems across at least two industries using permitted public primary or near-primary sources, starting with problems and existing workarounds rather than product concepts (operations/backlog/first-session.md).
summary: Three credible, distinct signals were documented: (1) prior-authorization paperwork in US medical practices (~13 hours per physician per week across two AMA survey years); (2) overdue invoices plus manual payment processes for invoicing US small businesses (59% carry 30+ day overdue invoices, vendor survey); (3) unplanned admin and manual inventory control in restaurants (44% of operators report 6+ unplanned GM admin hours weekly; counting/receiving errors drive variance). None of the three is validated; each record states its counterevidence and unknowns.
questions: Which administrative tasks consume small-business operators' time and money, with what measured evidence?
What workarounds and existing alternatives are already in use?
Where is the evidence strong, vendor-shaped, or missing the small-business segment entirely?

findings.text: Prior authorization is the strongest signal: two consecutive AMA physician surveys (2024, 2025) report ~39-40 requests and ~13 hours per physician per week, and 40% of practices employ dedicated prior-auth staff — an existing budget line, i.e. revealed willingness to pay for relief.

Overdue invoices are widespread among invoicing small businesses (59% at 30+ days, $17.7K average owed), and businesses name manual processes as the top internal cause of their own payment delays; the evidence is a single vendor source so far.
Restaurant unplanned admin and inventory variance are real but unevenly distributed, concentrated in lower-maturity operations; the benchmark sample underrepresents independent restaurants.

contradictory_findings.text: Each problem has a live mitigation path that shrinks its claimed size: insurer prior-auth reform pledges and ePA rules (burden so far unchanged), immediate-payment terms (largely avoid overdue invoices where markets allow), and process discipline/tool consistency in top restaurant operators.
Two of the three sources are vendor research with products to sell against the problem; only the AMA surveys are non-vendor, and they carry advocacy framing instead.

unresolved_questions: Small-practice distribution of prior-authorization time and task mix.
Independent corroboration of the late-payments picture (Federal Reserve SBCS, NFIB).
Owner/staff hours spent chasing payments (unquantified in current sources).
conclusions: Discovery quota met with three distinct, sourced signals across healthcare, cross-industry invoicing businesses, and restaurants; fewer-than-three was not necessary. No opportunity is validated and none is recommended for execution. Highest-value next investigation: the small-practice prior-authorization distribution question in the prior-authorization problem record — it pairs the strongest, twice-measured evidence with a revealed budget line (dedicated staff), and its answer decides whether the accessible customer is the small independent practice or a larger group.
next_steps: Open an investigation issue for the small-practice prior-authorization distribution question.
Corroborate late payments with Federal Reserve SBCS and NFIB sources.
Find independent-restaurant-specific evidence before deepening the restaurant problem.
Obtain independent review of these records via this session's PR.
